content.title: About
content.content: Cookie biscotti is a dry, crunchy Italian biscuit traditionally made from flour, sugar, eggs, butter, and nuts (most often almonds). It is baked twice, which gives it a dense, long‑lasting texture. Biscotti are commonly served with coffee or dessert wine and are meant to be dunked, softening the bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name biscotti comes from the Italian “biscotto,” meaning “twice‑baked.”
The classic recipe uses almonds, but modern versions include hazelnuts, pecans, chocolate chips, and dried fruit.
In Tuscany, biscotti are traditionally dipped in Vin Santo, a sweet dessert wine.
Because of their low moisture, biscotti can be stored for several weeks without spoiling.
Biscotti gained popularity in the United States in the 1970s thanks to Italian immigrants.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour and nuts provide dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Nuts add monounsaturated fats that are beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Almonds and vegetable oils supply vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: A balance of carbohydrates and a modest amount of protein offers quick and sustained energy.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Biscotti provide magnesium and phosphorus, important for muscle and bone function.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: Traditional biscotti contain almonds; those with nut allergies should choose nut‑free versions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet biscotti can raise blood sugar, so people with diabetes need to watch portion size.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Butter and sugar make biscotti relatively high in calories; moderation is key for weight management.

items.title: Gluten presence
items.content: Standard recipes use wheat flour, making them unsuitable for gluten‑free diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve biscotti with hot beverages—coffee, tea, or dessert wine—by dunking them briefly. They can be crushed and used as a base for cheesecakes, ice cream, or mixed into cake batter. As a snack, eat them whole, sometimes dusted with powdered sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep biscotti in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to prevent the fats from turning rancid. They typically stay fresh for 2–3 weeks.

fish-and-rice-with-mushroom-sauce.title: Fish and Rice with Mushroom Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of tender fish (commonly cod or salmon), steamed rice, and a flavorful mushroom sauce made from mushrooms, cream, and seasonings. It combines protein, complex carbohydrates, and healthy fats for a balanced meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mushroom sauce is often prepared with a reduction of broth and cream, giving it a rich, velvety texture.
Rice is usually cooked al dente so it holds its shape when mixed with the sauce.
The fish‑and‑mushroom combination is popular in Scandinavian and Eastern European cuisines.
A splash of white wine or soy sauce is sometimes added to deepen the sauce’s flavor.
The dish can be easily adapted for dietary needs by swapping dairy cream for plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Fish provides complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Fatty fish such as salmon contain omega‑3s that support heart and brain health.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice supplies steady‑release energy through its carbohydrate content.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms and fish are rich in B2, B3, and B6 vitamins, important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Mushrooms provide selenium and polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Fish or mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood or mushrooms.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the sauce includes soy sauce or broth, the sodium level can be high.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage of fish can lead to growth of harmful bacteria.

items.title: Dietary restrictions
items.content: Those limiting fat intake should choose lean fish and use low‑fat or plant‑based cream alternatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fish topped with mushroom sauce alongside a portion of steamed rice. Garnish with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or pair with a vegetable side for added color and nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a splash of broth or cream to prevent the sauce from drying out.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-poult.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce, Poultry and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: This is a home recipe for whole‑grain pasta tossed in a smooth cream sauce, pieces of poultry and a mix of vegetables. The dish is rich in fiber, protein and vitamins, while the cream sauce gives it a velvety texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta retains the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than refined white pasta.
The cream sauce can be made with low‑fat dairy or plant‑based alternatives to reduce saturated fat.
Poultry provides a highly digestible source of protein that supports muscle growth and repair.
Vegetables such as broccoli, carrots and bell pepper add antioxidants and fiber to the meal.
A homemade recipe lets you control salt and sugar levels, creating a healthier dish.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta supplies soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting healthy digestion and stable blood sugar.

items.title: Rich protein content
items.content: Chicken combined with whole‑grain pasta provides a complete amino‑acid profile beneficial for muscles and immunity.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables contribute vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium and folate, supporting skin, vision and cardiovascular health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta releases glucose more slowly, helping to control appetite and energy levels.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: A cream sauce made with a touch of olive oil or yogurt adds monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cream sauces can be salty; limit added salt especially for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑dense due to pasta and sauce; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Poultry must be cooked thoroughly to avoid the risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the cream sauce, poultry and vegetables. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan or a squeeze of lemon for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Keep the cream sauce separate if possible. Frozen portions can be kept for up to 1 month.

rice-brown-with-peas-fat-added.title: Brown Rice with Peas, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice with peas and added fat is a ready‑to‑eat product that contains whole grain brown rice, green peas and a small amount of vegetable oil to improve taste and aid absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins. It is commonly used in child nutrition, diet plans and as a quick side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, making it richer in fiber and minerals than white rice.
Peas are a good source of plant protein and vitamin C.
Adding a modest amount of fat increases the bioavailability of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
The rice‑pea combination provides a more balanced amino‑acid profile.
The product is widely used in institutional child‑feeding programs in Eastern Europe.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Brown rice supplies soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Peas add about 5 g of protein per 100 g of product, beneficial for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: The added vegetable oil provides energy and helps absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Rich in minerals and B‑vitamins
items.content: The product provides magnesium, phosphorus, iron and B‑vitamins that support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Brown rice has a lower GI than white rice, helping to control post‑meal glucose spikes.

items.title: Pea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Added fats increase the calorie density, so people monitoring intake should account for them.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption if consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Storage oxidation
items.content: Fat can oxidize over time, so the product should be stored in a cool, dry place.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready after heating in a microwave or on the stove. It can be served as a standalone dish, added to soups, salads, or used as a side for meat and fish. Fresh vegetables or herbs may be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. After opening, use within 3–4 days or refrigerate. Discard if a rancid odor develops.

sweet-potato-squash-pumpkin-chrysanthemu.title: Sweet potato, squash, pumpkin, chrysanthemum, or bean leaves, cooked

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato, squash, pumpkin, chrysanthemum leaves and bean leaves are vegetables and leafy greens commonly consumed after cooking. They are rich in vitamins, minerals, dietary fiber and antioxidants that support overall health.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potato belongs to the Convolvulaceae family, not to the true potato family.
Pumpkin has been cultivated for more than 7,000 years and is one of the oldest crops.
Modern zucchini was developed in Italy in the 16th century from wild squash varieties.
Chrysanthemum leaves are eaten as a vegetable in parts of Asia and are high in vitamins A and C.
Bean leaves, such as soybean leaves, are traditional ingredients in East Asian cuisine.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Pumpkin and sweet potato contain high levels of beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A for eye health and immunity.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Squash and bean leaves provide vitamin C, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: All listed vegetables are good sources of soluble and insoluble fiber, aiding digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Pumpkin and bean leaves supply potassium, magnesium and iron, essential for heart and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Chrysanthemum leaves and sweet potato contain flavonoids and polyphenols that may reduce the risk of chronic diseases.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to bean leaves or chrysanthemum.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Bean leaves and certain pumpkin varieties contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation if consumed in excess.

items.title: High starch content
items.content: Sweet potato has a relatively high glycemic index; people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Toxic parts
items.content: Pumpkin seeds and chrysanthemum stems may contain bitter compounds; only eat the approved edible parts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Vegetables can be boiled, steamed, roasted or stewed. Sweet potatoes are often baked in wedges, squash is sautéed, pumpkin is used in soups and purées, chrysanthemum leaves are blanched for salads, and bean leaves are added to stir‑fries or used as a filling for pancakes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh vegetables in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer, loosely packed in a perforated bag. Cooked dishes should be stored in airtight containers in the fridge and consumed within 3‑4 days.
